question: Is God the author of confusion?
summary: 1 Corinthians 14:33 states flatly that God is not the author of confusion. But Genesis 11:7-9 has Yahweh deliberately confounding human language at Babel so the people will not understand one another, and 1 Corinthians 1:27 has God choosing foolish things specifically to confound the wise. The same epistle that denies confusion also describes God deploying it.

reconcile.connective: Clarke and JFB read each "confound" in its own sense — 14:33's akatastasia names worship disorder, not the shaming Paul intends in 1:27.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells' Skeptic's Annotated Bible pairs Babel's language-confounding and 1:27's confounding of the wise directly against 14:33's flat denial.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells

pd_work.resource: Adam Clarke, Commentary on the Bible (1832), on 1 Corinthians 14:33
pd_work.author: Adam Clarke
pd_work.note: Clarke, already surfaced on this row, glosses 'confusion' in 14:33 as the Greek akatastasia -- 'tumult, sedition,' i.e. competing, disorderly speech in worship -- not confusion in any general sense, the same narrowing move that answers the Babel and 1:27 legs of this tension. John Haley's Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874) was checked (curl+grep of the full djvu text): it quotes 1 Corinthians 14:33 verbatim in its 'Holiness' section's 'God the Author of Evil / Not the Author of Evil' table (Part II, Ch. I, pp. 76-78), applying the identical narrower-sense-of-the-word method to Ezekiel 20:25 and Amos 3:6, but that table never treats Genesis 11:7-9 or 1 Corinthians 1:27, so Clarke -- keyed to the specific 'confusion' wording this row turns on -- is used as the primary defense source.

link.title: CARM: If God is not the author of confusion, what about the Tower of Babel?
link.note: Live apologetic treatment addressing all three legs (Babel, 1 Cor 1:27, 1 Cor 14:33) by distinguishing God's judgment on human pride from God's orderly nature within the church.

excerpts.attribution: Adam Clarke, Commentary on the Bible (1832)
excerpts.excerpt_text: For God is not the author of confusion - Let not the persons who act in the congregation in this disorderly manner, say, that they are under the influence of God; for he is not the author of confusion; but two, three, or more, praying or teaching in the same place, at the same time, is confusion; and God is not the author of such work; and let men beware how they attribute such disorder to the God of order and peace. The apostle calls such conduct ακαταστασια, tumult, sedition; and such it is in the sight of God, and in the sight of all good men.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Names the Greek word behind 'confusion' in 14:33 as akatastasia (tumult, sedition) and confines it to disorderly, simultaneous speaking in worship — narrowing the term the skeptic reads as an absolute denial that God ever causes any confusion of any kind.
excerpts.source_note_text: For God is not the author of confusion - Let not the persons who act in the congregation in this disorderly manner, say, that they are under the influence of God; for he is not the author of confusion; but two, three, or more, praying or teaching in the same place, at the same time, is confusion; and God is not the author of such work; and let men beware how they attribute such disorder to the God of order and peace. The apostle calls such conduct ακαταστασια, tumult, sedition; and such it is in the sight of God, and in the sight of all good men. How often is a work of God marred and discredited by the folly of men! for nature will always, and Satan too, mingle themselves as far as they can in the genuine work of the Spirit, in order to discredit and destroy it. Nevertheless, in great revivals of religion it is almost impossible to prevent wild - fire from getting in amongst the true fire; but it is the duty of the ministers of God to watch against and prudently check this; but if themselves encourage it, then there will be confusion and every evil work.
